nameStory: Leiobunum nigropalpi gets its scientific name from two Latin words: 'nigropalpi' means 'black palps,' referring to the dark coloring of its palps (the small feeding appendages near its mouth). Like other harvestmen, it's often called a 'daddy longlegs' because of its impossibly thin, long legs that seem almost thread-like.
description: This harvestman is one of the classic 'daddy longlegs' arachnids you'll encounter in New England forests and gardens. It has the typical harvestman body plan: a small, oval body with eight extremely long, thin legs that can span several inches. Unlike spiders, harvestmen have their body segments fused together into what looks like a single unit, and they don't spin webs or have venomous fangs. The body is usually brownish or grayish, often with subtle patterns that help it blend into bark and leaf litter.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, compact oval body that feels firm to the touch, with all segments fused together unlike spiders which have a clear waist between front and back sections

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark-colored palps (small mouth appendages) that stand out against the lighter body - look for these black feeding parts near the front when viewed up close

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body typically pea-sized or smaller, but leg span can reach 2-3 inches when fully extended - legs feel surprisingly delicate and hair-thin

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic bouncing gait and will often freeze motionless when disturbed, then suddenly scurry away in jerky movements

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Extremely long, thread-like legs that easily break off when handled - the detached legs may continue twitching for several minutes as a defense mechanism

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly in areas with rich leaf litter and decaying wood. They favor moist microhabitats like under logs, in brush piles, and among fallen leaves where humidity stays higher. You'll also spot them on tree trunks and wooden structures like fence posts and building foundations, especially during evening hours.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and leaf litter. Look for them on warm, humid evenings in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily observed hunting for small insects and scavenging. Most mating and egg-laying occurs during warm summer months.
seasonality.fall: Still active through early fall, often seen congregating on buildings and tree trunks. They're building up energy reserves before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off after first hard frosts, though some may survive in protected microhabitats. Eggs overwinter in soil and leaf litter.

funFact: When a harvestman loses a leg to a predator, the detached leg continues to twitch and move for up to an hour, acting like a writhing decoy while the harvestman escapes - and unlike spiders, they can't regenerate the lost limb, so they're stuck with seven legs for life!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Leiobunum harvestmen, which all look remarkably similar. The key is to look closely at the palps near the mouth - nigropalpi has distinctly dark, almost black palps while many relatives have lighter-colored ones. Remember: 'Nigropalpi = black palps' to keep it straight.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'daddy longlegs,' harvestmen are not spiders and the common myth about them being extremely venomous but unable to bite humans is completely false - they have no venom at all and aren't even closely related to spiders, belonging to a completely different order of arachnids.
compareHints: Among its Leiobunum relatives in New England, nigropalpi is distinguished primarily by its dark palps, while the Eastern Harvestman (L. vittatum) has a distinctive dark stripe down its back and lighter palps. The Golden Harvestman (L. flavum) has a more yellowish coloration overall, and the Warty Harvestman (L. verrucosum) has a distinctly bumpy, textured body surface that feels rough to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Eastern Harvestman is one of the most common Leiobunum species in New England and tends to be more uniformly brown than its relatives.
Aldrich's Harvestman is very difficult to distinguish from its close relatives like the Eastern Harvestman without examining fine details under magnification.

Among its Leiobunum relatives, the Warty Harvestman is the only one with pronounced bumpy texture on its body - the Eastern Harvestman and other cousins have smooth, unmarked backs that feel sleek to the touch.

Among its Leiobunum relatives in New England, the Polished Harvestman stands out for its exceptionally smooth, glossy body surface - the Eastern Harvestman has a more matte finish, while the Warty Harvestman lives up to its name with obvious bumps and texture.
Distinguishing Leiobunum calcar from other harvestmen in its genus requires close examination of subtle features like leg length ratios and body markings.
Distinguishing this species from other Leiobunum harvestmen requires close examination of details like leg proportions and body markings that aren't easily visible in the field.
Among the Leiobunum harvestmen in New England, the Golden Harvestman is the only one with that distinctive golden-yellow body coloration.
Leiobunum formosum can be distinguished from its common relative the Eastern Harvestman by its notably glossier, more reflective body surface and slightly more compact build.
Distinguishing this species from its more common Leiobunum relatives requires close examination of subtle features like leg proportions and body markings that are difficult to see in the field.
